slides.title: GateLite: Sparse Gated Adapters for Low-Resource Speech Recognition
subtitle: A. Example and B. Sample
Synthetic example paper - interface demo only
slides.notes: Introduce the problem in one sentence: adapting big speech encoders when a language has only a few hours of data.
slides.transition: Start from the data regime we all work in.

slides.title: Outline: problem, idea, results, recommendation
bullets: Problem: full fine-tuning overfits on little data
Idea: route each frame to 2 of 8 small experts
Results: the gain is largest with the least data
Limits and a recommendation for our languages
slides.notes: Tell the lab what decision we will reach at the end, so they listen to the results with that question in mind.
slides.transition: Start with the data regime we all work in.

slides.title: Full fine-tuning overfits when a language has under 10 h of labelled speech

bullets.text: Encoders are pre-trained on high-resource data, then adapted per language
A 300M-parameter encoder overfits with only a few hours of transcribed speech
Dense adapters spend capacity on every frame, even the easy ones

slides.notes: Stress the data regime: under 10 hours. Ask the audience how many of their languages fall below that.
slides.transition: So how do we adapt cheaply without overfitting?
slides.key_message: Below 10 h of labelled speech, full fine-tuning overfits

slides.title: GateLite routes each frame to 2 of 8 small adapter experts
bullets: Sparse gated adapter: **2 of 8** experts active per frame
Load-balancing regulariser keeps expert usage uniform
Evaluated on five languages with 1 to 50 h of training data
slides.notes: These are the three contributions as the paper states them; the next slide shows the block.
slides.key_message: Only 2 of 8 small experts work on each frame
slides.transition: Here is where the experts sit in the encoder.

slides.title: A router picks the top-2 of 8 bottleneck experts after each of the 24 frozen layers

bullets.text: Only adapters and the CTC head are trained

slides.notes: Walk left to right through the figure. It is a schematic, not a result.
slides.key_message: The encoder stays frozen; only adapters and the CTC head train
slides.transition: Does this beat what we use today?

slides.title: At 10 h, GateLite has the lowest average WER: 27.9% vs 31.4% for full fine-tuning

table.caption: Average WER (%) on five languages, 10 h of training data

slides.notes: Point at the last row. The trained-parameter column matters: GateLite trains fewer parameters than the dense adapter.
slides.key_message: GateLite gives the lowest WER at 10 h with fewer trained parameters than a dense adapter
slides.transition: And how does the gap change with more data?
if_asked: more parameters? dense adapter trains 4.0% and is still worse (29.1)

slides.title: The gain is largest with little data and nearly vanishes at 50 h
slides.notes: Redrawn from the CSV behind Figure 2. At 50 h the two bars differ by 0.2 points.
slides.key_message: The gain is large at 1-5 h and vanishes at 50 h

slides.title: Only read speech was tested, and routing costs 6% latency

bullets.text: Routing adds 6% inference latency on a single GPU

slides.key_message: Untested on spontaneous speech; routing costs 6% latency

slides.title: Recommendation: try GateLite on our languages with under 10 h of data

bullets.text: Biggest benefit in the lowest-data regime
Negligible at 50 h of training data

slides.notes: End with the decision we need: pick two languages under 10 h and compare against our dense adapter.
